title: Aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING and window functions

videos.script: Every question anybody actually asks a database is a summary. Not show me the orders — how many, how much, per what. {{summary}} This lesson is the two ways to answer that, and they are genuinely different tools that look similar enough to be confused for years. {{two}} The first collapses. Group by customer and a thousand rows become one row per customer — you get the totals and you lose the orders. That is GROUP BY, and it is the one everybody learns. {{collapse}} The second does not collapse. Every row stays, and beside it appears something computed from its neighbours: the running total, the customer's average, this order's rank among theirs. {{window}} That is a window function, and it answers the questions people quietly give up on — how does this row compare, what came before it, is it in the top three of its group. Before they existed you wrote a subquery per column. {{questions}} And between the two sits the thing that catches everybody. AVG ignores the rows where the value is unknown. So the average is not the sum divided by the number of rows, and it never was — and nothing in the output says which rows it counted. {{avg}}
